item.title: Solvent-Free Synthesis of Highly Luminescent Solid-State Boric Acid-Assisted Carbon Dots for Stable and High-Contrast Latent Fingerprint Visualization
item.description:
Abstract
The development of efficient, stable, and environmentally friendly fluorescent materials for latent fingerprint visualization remains a major challenge in forensic science. Carbon dots (CDs) have emerged as promising fluorescent nanomaterials owing to their low toxicity, tunable optical properties, and eco-friendly nature. However, their practical application in solid-state systems is often hindered by aggregation-induced quenching (AIQ), which can significantly suppress fluorescence emission. In this study, highly luminescent boric acid-assisted carbon dots (B-CDs) were synthesized through a simple, rapid, and solvent-free thermal process using citric acid, urea, and boric acid as precursors. Unlike conventional approaches, the developed method enables the direct formation of solid-state emissive carbon dot powders without requiring additional surface passivation, purification, or polymeric matrices. Structural and spectroscopic characterizations supported the successful formation of heteroatom-functionalized B-CDs that exhibit excitation-dependent photoluminescence and strong solid-state emission. The synthesized B-CDs exhibited a high solid-state photoluminescence quantum yield of 77.5%. The B-CDs showed strong short-term stability, retaining more than 95% of their initial PL intensity after 60 min exposure to 95% relative humidity and during short-term thermal treatment up to 90 °C. Long-term measurements showed approximately 57% PL retention after 5 days at 95% relative humidity and approximately 48% after 5 days of thermal aging at 50 °C, while approximately 92% of the initial PL intensity was retained after 5 days of continuous UV irradiation. The proposed solvent-free synthesis strategy offers a simple and potentially scalable route for producing strongly emissive solid-state carbon dots, highlighting their potential for latent fingerprint visualization.

item.title: Electronic Spectroscopy of Atomic Defects in Molybdenum Disulfide under Ambient Conditions
item.description:
Abstract
We present results of electronic spectroscopy experiments performed on individual defects in the prototypical transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) under ambient conditions by way of conductive atomic force microscopy (C-AFM). Data acquired in the form of consecutive, high-resolution current maps at various bias voltages allow the assessment of local conductivity and differential conductance as a function of bias voltage for individual defects, the effects of which range from single-atomic sites to several nanometers in lateral size. Characteristic behavior in spectroscopy data allows the categorization of observed defects into distinct groups and provides clues with regard to their chemical identities.

item.title: Optimal and Secure Operation of a μ-CHP Solid Oxide Fuel Cell System
item.description:
Abstract
Performance optimization and operational safety of solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC) systems are crucial for long-term operation and lifespan prolongation. However, optimal and secure operation under real-world conditions remains challenging. This study demonstrates a fast constraint-adaptation real-time optimization methodology that optimizes the electrical and combined-heat-and-power (CHP) efficiencies of a μ-CHP SOFC system across power targets, using transient measurements and a simplified dynamic model despite significant plant-model mismatch. The algorithm converged to power targets within four iterations (15 min), achieving at least 5% relative improvement in electrical efficiency through multi-input manipulation. Optimizing CHP efficiency increased hot water production by 20%. The algorithm remained robust against natural gas grid fluctuations and programmed control-subsystem interruptions while maintaining secure operation without safety shutdowns, demonstrating its maturity for optimal and safe operation of real-world SOFC systems.

item.title: Terahertz Spectroscopy-Enabled Smart Monitoring of Drug Salt Synthesis: A Case Study on 8-Hydroquinolinium Salicylate
item.description:
Abstract
While salt formation is a proven strategy to overcome poor aqueous solubility and facilitate the development of active pharmaceutical ingredients, real-time monitoring of this process still lacks molecular-resolution process analytical technology (PAT). Using 8-hydroxyquinolinium salicylate as a model system, this study integrates cryogenic terahertz spectroscopy, Born–Oppenheimer molecular dynamics (BOMD), and interpretable deep learning to develop a terahertz time-domain spectroscopy (THz-TDS) workflow for stage-resolved monitoring of pharmaceutical salt formation. THz measurements (80 ∼300 K) revealed the anharmonic character of the lattice vibrations, whose dominant features were reproduced and assigned by BOMD simulations. Umbrella sampling indicated a nearly barrierless proton-transfer process (ΔG‡ = 1.7 kcal/mol) with picosecond-scale shuttling dynamics. Statistical analysis of ten kinetic models confirms first-order conversion (AIC = −151.2; n = 0.99 ± 0.02) and yielded an Arrhenius activation energy of 45.2 ± 2.3 kJ/mol for predictive process optimization. Dissolution data (n = 3; mean ± SD) showed a statistically significant 2.0–2.6-fold enhancement across pH 1.2, 6.8, and 7.4, as assessed by Welch’s t test and two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s HSD test (p < 0.001). The interpretable CNN achieved 98.2% hold-out test accuracy and used SHAP to link decisions to chemical fingerprint bands. Overfitting was evaluated through spectral dimensionality reduction, dropout, a stratified training/test split, 5-fold cross-validation, leave-one-batch-out cross-validation, and external batches under shifted thermal conditions, with accuracy retained at ≥ 92.7%. These results support a proof-of-concept, interpretable THz-TDS PAT workflow with molecular-level resolution.

item.title: Machine Learning-Driven Prediction and Optimization of Thermoelectric Transport Properties in Ce-Doped CaMnO 3 Ceramics
item.description:
Abstract
Oxide-based thermoelectric materials are promising candidates for high-temperature waste heat recovery owing to their excellent thermal and chemical stability. Nevertheless, optimizing their thermoelectric performance remains challenging because electrical resistivity and the Seebeck coefficient exhibit complex, nonlinear, and composition-dependent relationships. In this work, experimental measurements combined with data-driven machine learning approaches were employed to predict and optimize the high-temperature thermoelectric behavior of Ce-doped CaMnO3 (Ca1–xCexMnO3, x = 0.02–0.10) ceramics using Support Vector Machine (SVM), Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and a hybrid Convolutional Neural Network–Long Short-term Memory (CNN–LSTM) architecture. The models were trained and validated using experimentally measured electrical resistivity (ρ) and Seebeck coefficient (S) data collected over the temperature range of 50–800 °C. Among the investigated approaches, the hybrid CNN–LSTM model, which uniquely combines spatial feature extraction with sequential learning to resolve complex nonlinear transport behaviors that conventional machine-learning models fail to capture accurately, exhibited the highest predictive performance, achieving coefficients of determination (R2) of 0.9982 for electrical resistivity and 0.9987 for the Seebeck coefficient. Permutation feature importance analysis further revealed that the Ce concentration has a stronger influence on the transport properties than the operating temperature. To identify the optimum operating conditions, 150,000 Monte Carlo simulations were performed using the trained CNN–LSTM model to generate continuous multidimensional response surfaces. The optimization results identified a favorable thermoelectric region at a Ce content of x = 0.05–0.06 and temperatures between 350 and 500 °C, where the simulated power factor exceeded 0.35 mW/K2m. These results demonstrate the potential of hybrid deep learning for data-driven analysis and optimization of oxide-based thermoelectric materials under the investigated experimental conditions.

item.title: Plasma-Enhanced Electrostatic Precipitator (ESP) with Self-Cleaning Electrode for Scalable Remediation of Particulate Matter in Large Diesel Engines
item.description:
Abstract
We have demonstrated a fundamentally new pollution control device that integrates a plasma-enhanced electrostatic precipitator (PE-ESP) with a self-cleaning electrode. In the PE-ESP, high-voltage (20 kV) nanosecond (20 ns) pulses generate a transient plasma that produces ion densities approximately 6 orders of magnitude higher than those created by a conventional DC corona. This plasma enhancement increases the particle charging efficiency and allows electrostatic precipitators to be designed much more compactly, making them suitable for mobile sources. Using the PE-ESP, we were able to remove more than 90% of diesel particulate matter while consuming 1% of the available engine power. A key element of this innovation is the soot-collecting electrode, which consists of a highly porous stainless-steel material that can be electrically regenerated using Joule heating to burn off accumulated soot, converting it to CO2. This self-cleaning soot-collecting electrode has been tested through four accumulation–regeneration cycles, demonstrating more than 200 h of reliable operation while maintaining removal efficiencies above 89%. This approach addresses the main challenges associated with conventional emission-control technologies. For example, diesel particulate filters (DPFs) achieve high removal efficiency but create significant engine backpressure, which becomes problematic for large diesel engines. Electrostatic precipitators (ESPs) typically avoid flow restriction, but have historically been too large for mobile sources or high-power engines such as those used in marine vessels or locomotives. We believe this system is the first of its kind and is scalable to large diesel engines in the one-megawatt class and beyond, where no acceptable pollution-remediation solutions currently exist.

item.title: Nb-Doped g-C 3 N 4 : A Highly Efficient and Stable Catalyst for Oxidative Desulfurization
item.description:
Abstract
This study reports the synthesis and application of niobium-doped graphitic carbon nitride as a high-performance catalyst for oxidative desulfurization (ODS) of fuels. The 10-NbCN material, prepared via pyrolysis, exhibits Nb species that are highly dispersed at the atomic level within the g-C3N4 framework, as confirmed by XRD, FTIR, and TEM. Under optimized conditions (60 °C, O/S = 20:1, 4 g L–1 catalyst), 96% removal of dibenzothiophene (DBT) is achieved within 120 min, outperforming pure g-C3N4 and Nb2O5. Kinetic studies reveal pseudo-first-order behavior with an activation energy of 41.2 kJ mol–1. Remarkably, quinoline enhances DBT conversion even at high concentrations, indicating an unusual tolerance to nitrogen-containing compounds typically known to inhibit ODS systems. Evaluation in real diesel confirms that 10-NbCN selectively removes sulfur compounds while preserving the hydrocarbon matrix. EPR and DFT results suggest that Nb sites efficiently activate H2O2, promoting the generation of reactive oxygen species. The catalyst demonstrates outstanding stability over six cycles with negligible Nb leaching, supported by the preservation of Nb–N coordination under oxidative conditions. These findings highlight Nb–g-C3N4 as a robust and N-tolerant catalyst for ultralow sulfur fuel production.

item.title: Influence of Glutaraldehyde on the Properties of Agar-Based Films
item.description:
Abstract
Biopolymers have been used as alternatives to fossil-derived polymers. In this context, agar, a polysaccharide extracted from seaweed, has stood out due to its properties in the formulation of polymeric films. In this work, agar was used in combination with glycerol and glutaraldehyde to formulate polymeric films by the casting method with water as solvent. The films produced were characterized regarding their water interactions using swelling, solubility, and contact angle tests. Mechanical and physical properties were determined using a tensile test and thickness measurements. Optical microscopy was used to analyze the surface, and scanning electron microscopy was used to analyze the surface and cross-section of the films. Spectroscopic properties were obtained by Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) and ultraviolet–visible spectroscopy. Thermal degradation was determined by thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). It was possible to produce polymeric films with a thickness of around 120 μm and mechanical properties like those found on low-density polyethylene, showing tensile strengths of 15–16 MPa. The solubility of the material was 42% and the swelling ranged between 349–555%, depending on the concentration of glutaraldehyde added to the film formulation of films. Adding glutaraldehyde altered the surface characteristics of the films while maintaining the other properties. However, no evidence of cross-linking reactions was found.

item.title: Chloride Transport Resistance, Concrete Cover Performance, and Service-Life Assessment of Reinforced Concrete under Brazilian Durability Requirements
item.description:
Abstract
Chloride-induced corrosion is one of the main causes of premature deterioration in reinforced concrete structures exposed to marine and industrial environments. In such conditions, durability depends not only on the quality and transport resistance of the cementitious matrix but also on the adequacy of the reinforcement cover thickness. Although ABNT NBR 6118:2026 prescribes minimum concrete cover requirements according to environmental exposure classes, experimental validations of these recommendations under severe chloride exposure conditions remain limited. This study evaluates the effectiveness of the minimum reinforcement cover thicknesses specified for high environmental aggressiveness classes (EC III and EC IV) through accelerated chloride migration testing and the analysis of concrete quality parameters. Concrete specimens were produced using ordinary Portland cement (PC V ARI RS) with water-to-cement (w/c) ratios ranging from 0.43 to 0.68. The experimental program included compressive strength, ultrasonic pulse velocity (UPV), water absorption, void index, chloride penetration depth, and non-steady-state chloride migration coefficient (Dns) measurements. Chloride penetration fronts were determined by colorimetric analysis after accelerated migration testing and compared with the nominal concrete cover thicknesses prescribed by ABNT NBR 6118:2026. The results demonstrated that all investigated mixtures presented chloride penetration depths lower than the minimum cover thicknesses specified for EC III and EC IV, even for concretes that exceeded the maximum w/c ratio limits established by the standard, indicating the conservative nature of the Brazilian prescriptive durability approach. Chloride penetration depths decreased from approximately 25 mm to 13 mm as the w/c ratio decreased, while Dns values were reduced from 12.08 × 10–12 to 4.11 × 10–12 m2/s, indicating substantial improvements in chloride transport resistance due to matrix densification and reduced transport pathways. Strong correlations were observed between chloride penetration behavior and Dns, compressive strength, void index, and UPV, demonstrating the influence of pore connectivity and internal concrete quality on chloride transport. Additionally, the experimentally obtained Dns values allowed comparative interpretations regarding the long-term chloride resistance and potential service-life performance of the investigated concretes.

item.title: Design and Preclinical Evaluation of Two Prostate-Specific Membrane Antigen-Targeting Trifluoroborate Derivatives Suitable for One-Step Radiofluorination
item.description:
Abstract
Prostate cancer was the most frequently diagnosed cancer and the second leading cause of cancer-related death among men in the United States in 2025. Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)-targeted PET tracers have significantly improved the detection, visualization, and staging of prostate cancer. Recently, the novel prosthetic group [18F]AmBF3-Tz was introduced, combining simple isotopic 18F-radiolabeling of alkylammoniomethyltrifluoroborates (AmBF3) with efficient bioorthogonal tetrazine-trans-cyclooctene (TCO) conjugation. This study evaluated the suitability of [18F]AmBF3-Tz for radiolabeling PSMA-targeting urea derivatives and assessed its impact on PSMA-binding affinity in vitro and in vivo. Four precursors─TCO-PSMA, TCO-tranexamic acid-PSMA, AmBF3-PSMA, and AmBF3-tranexamic acid-PSMA─were synthesized and used for the preparation of [18F]AmBF3-PSMA and [18F]AmBF3-tranexamic acid-PSMA via one-step or two-step labeling strategies. Conjugation before radiolabeling gave radiochemical yields of 5.2–11.8%, whereas the two-step method gave 0.7–9.8%. Although these yields demonstrate feasibility, they are lower and more variable than the 33 ± 5% yield obtained for [18F]AmBF3-Tz and would require substantial optimization before clinical translation. Overall, [18F]AmBF3-PSMA and [18F]AmBF3-tranexamic acid-PSMA demonstrated PSMA-specific tumor uptake and enabled the visualization of C4-2 xenografts. The tranexamic acid-containing tracer showed higher tumor-to-background ratios than [18F]AmBF3-PSMA in this study, but the absolute tumor uptake was not significantly different between the two tracers. The moderate and variable radiochemical yields, microscale reaction sensitivity, and small animal group sizes indicate that this proof-of-concept platform warrants further optimization before its suitability for clinical translation can be assessed.

item.title: Effects of Low-Intensity Exercise on Exhaled Breath Condensate Biomarkers in Healthy Horses
item.description:
Abstract
Exhaled breath condensate (EBC) has emerged as a promising diagnostic tool for equine respiratory disease. However, the influence of exercise on the biomarkers of EBC remains unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the influence of low-intensity exercise on EBC biomarkers (hydrogen peroxide, pH, and nitrite) in healthy horses and to assess the feasibility of postexercise sample collection under real-world conditions. Twenty clinically healthy horses (ten Quarter Horses and ten Brazilian Sport Horses) were evaluated. Respiratory rate (RR) and heart rate (HR) were recorded at rest, followed by EBC collection using a collector developed by our research group. Horses then performed 10 min of trotting, low-intensity protocol, after which RR, HR, and EBC samples were reassessed. Upper airway endoscopy and tracheal lavage with differential cytology confirmed respiratory health. Biomarker concentrations were analyzed by using appropriate parametric tests. Light exercise significantly increased RR, HR, and EBC sample volumes (p < 0.05). Sample volume evidenced a weak association with ambient temperature (p = 0.014, r = 0.186) and relative humidity (p = 0.010, r = 0.218). Exercise did not significantly affect pH (p = 0.380), hydrogen peroxide (p = 0.152), or nitrite (p = 0.218). Nitrite was negatively associated with ambient temperature (p = 0.023, r = −0.056) and relative humidity (p < 0.001, r = −0.428) and evidenced a moderate positive association with hydrogen peroxide in postexercise (p = 0.004, r = 0.611). Under the conditions evaluated, light exercise did not alter equine EBC biomarker concentrations, supporting the feasibility of postexercise sampling.

item.title: Two New Metabolites from Moquiniastrum sordidum : Phytochemical Characterization and Multifaceted Bioactivity
item.description:
Abstract
Recent taxonomic revisions based on molecular phylogenetics transferred species from Gochnatia to Moquiniastrum, which now includes 22 species, 20 of which occur in Brazil with an extra-Amazonian distribution. Here, we report a phytochemical study of Moquiniastrum sordidum (Less.) G. Sancho. Chromatographic separation afforded eight compounds, including two new metabolites: a sesquiterpene (5) and a phenolic glycoside (8). The known compounds were identified as simiarenol (1), oleanolic acid (2), hispidulin (3), tyrosol (4), genkwanin (6), and apigenin (7). The relative configuration of compound 5 was established using pip-HSQMBC-IPAP NMR, which afforded accurate long-range 2,3JCH coupling constants. Dereplication enabled the putative annotation of 45 metabolites: 12 flavonoids, 10 chlorogenic acid derivatives, 5 hydroxycinnamic acid derivatives, 9 terpenes, and 9 others. The biological potential of the extracts and isolated metabolites was evaluated using antioxidant, cytotoxic, antimicrobial, and antileishmanial assays. The new phenolic glycoside (8) showed potent antioxidant activity (ABTS: 1111 μmol TE g–1; FRAP: 4293 μmol Fe(II) g–1). Oleanolic acid (MIC = 130 μg mL–1) and apigenin (MIC = 30 μg mL–1) showed activity against the Gram-positive bacterium Bacillus cereus. Preliminary cytotoxic screening against HCT-116 cells showed that the dichloromethane fraction inhibited proliferation by 92% at 50 μg mL–1. Antileishmanial evaluation revealed moderate activity of the crude extract, which was significantly enhanced upon fractionation, with the dichloromethane fraction showing the highest activity against intracellular amastigotes (IC50 = 8.23 μg mL–1; SI = 7.87), indicating a selective antiparasitic effect.

item.title: Recovery of Citric Acid from Fermentation Broth Using Supported Ionic Liquids
item.description:
Abstract
Citric acid is widely used in the pharmaceutical, food, and cosmetic industries. However, the recovery of bioproduced citric acid from fermentation broths typically involves purification steps that generate substantial waste. This work proposes an alternative recovery strategy based on the selective adsorption of citric acid using supported ionic liquids (SILs). Two SILs were prepared by immobilizing the IL ligands diethylpropylethanolammonium chloride ([Si][N3222OH]Cl) and 1-propyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride ([Si][C3C1Im]Cl) onto a solid silica support. The materials were characterized by 13C NMR spectroscopy, elemental analysis, and determination of the specific surface area (SBET). Batch adsorption experiments were conducted to evaluate the effects of contact time, initial citric acid concentration, temperature, and pH. Adsorption kinetics were analyzed using pseudo-first-order, pseudo-second-order, intraparticle diffusion, and Boyd models, while equilibrium data were interpreted using the Langmuir, Freundlich, and Dubinin–Radushkevich isotherm models. The pseudo-second-order model best described the adsorption kinetics, whereas the Freundlich model provided the best fit for the equilibrium data. Maximum adsorption capacities of 577 and 793 mg·g–1 were obtained for [Si][N3222OH]Cl and [Si][C3C1Im]Cl, respectively. Reusability of the SILs was also assessed through successive adsorption–desorption cycles. The SILs enabled a citric acid desorption range of 43.8% to 100%. Finally, the materials were applied to the recovery of citric acid directly from a fermentation broth to evaluate their potential for industrial application. Overall, these results highlight the potential of SILs as promising adsorbent materials for the efficient recovery of citric acid from fermentation broths, paving the way for their widespread use at the industrial scale.

item.title: Effects of α-Linolenic Acid and Arachidonic Acid on the Cytotoxicity and Steatosis of HepG2 Cells
item.description:
Abstract
Hepatic steatosis, characterized by excessive triglyceride (TG) accumulation in hepatocytes, serves as the initiating event in the early phase of metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD). Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) exert differential modulatory effects on hepatic steatosis, but the underlying lipidomic remodeling remains incompletely understood. In this study, we systematically investigated the impacts of α-linolenic acid (ALA) and arachidonic acid (AA) on lipid accumulation, inflammation, and cytotoxicity in fattyacid-induced HepG2 cells. Our data indicated that ALA at concentrations >300 μM and AA at >150 μM significantly inhibited cell viability. In fatty acid-induced steatotic HepG2 cells, 100 μM ALA significantly reduced both triglyceride (TG) and total cholesterol (TC) levels, whereas 100 μM AA significantly increased TG levels without affecting TC content. Furthermore, quantitative real-time PCR revealed that 100 μM ALA significantly downregulated the transcriptional expression of NF-κB, TNF-α, and IL-6, while 100 μM AA upregulated the expression of these three factors. The untargeted metabolomic profiling and KEGG pathway enrichment analysis showed that ALA significantly modulated glycerophospholipid metabolism, amino acid metabolism, nucleotide metabolism, and central carbon metabolism in steatotic HepG2 cells. Lipidomics analysis further demonstrated that ALA, through conversion to DHA and EPA, remodeled TG molecular species and was incorporated into multiple membrane phospholipids. Furthermore, Drug Affinity Responsive Target Stability (DARTS) and molecular docking results indicated that choline kinase α (CHKA) might be a potential target of ALA in HepG2 cells. Conclusively, ALA might contribute to the progression of hepatocyte steatosis by remodeling TG molecular species, incorporating into membrane phospholipids, modulating glycerophospholipid metabolism, and targeting CHKA.

item.title: Fracture-Influenced Seepage Behavior and Storage Capacity of Compressed Air Energy Storage in Closed Mine Roadways under Cyclic Operation
item.description:
Abstract
Repurposing roadways in closed coal mines for compressed air energy storage (CAES) offers a promising route for resource recycling and large-scale energy storage. Frequent rapid charging–discharging triggers cyclic temperature–pressure fluctuations in surrounding rock and causes air-leakage risks for underground CAES facilities. This work investigates air-leakage behaviors and thermo-hydro-mechanical (THM) coupling responses of CAES in closed mine roadways. Based on mass-energy conservation, a THM coupled numerical framework integrated with a fracture-growth permeability model is established to describe gas migration, pore-pressure evolution and convective heat transfer. Series of numerical simulations are carried out to quantify the effects of cavern initial temperature, gas-injection temperature, injection rate, initial surrounding-rock damage degree, operation cycles and injected-gas type on system performance. The results indicate that cavern pressure rises nearly linearly during charging and declines steadily during discharging. Compression induces rapid gas-temperature growth, which later decreases via heat exchange with surrounding rock. According to single-factor sensitivity analysis, the injected gas type (relative contribution of 32.92%), initial rock-mass damage (30.01%), and number of cycles (29.78%) are the three dominant factors governing gas-leakage magnitude. Reservoir temperature, gas injection rate and injected-gas temperature exhibit relatively limited influences under the investigated conditions. After 100 continuous charging–discharging cycles, the cavern gas density decreases by approximately 12%. Under identical conditions, hydrogen yields larger leakage mass flux than air and carbon dioxide, whereas carbon dioxide obtains higher equilibrium pressure. This study reveals the coupling mechanism between air leakage and thermodynamic responses for roadway-based CAES and advances multiphysics coupling theories for mine-related energy storage. The obtained results offer theoretical insights into the leakage-thermodynamic coupling mechanism of abandoned-roadway CAES.

item.title: HierDTA: Hierarchical Structure-Aware Representation Learning for Drug–Target Affinity Prediction
item.description:
Abstract
Drug–target affinity (DTA) prediction plays an important role in computer-aided drug discovery, where reliable computational models can help prioritize compound–protein pairs before experimental validation. A key challenge in DTA prediction is to effectively mine multilevel molecular information from drug structures while accurately modeling the binding-site environment of target proteins. To address these issues, we introduce HierDTA, a hierarchical structure-aware framework for DTA prediction. HierDTA represents each drug as an atom–motif heterogeneous graph and introduces an augmentation module that propagates functional-motif semantics to the corresponding atoms. For proteins, kinase domain structures are converted into residue interaction graphs. The resulting atom and residue representations are integrated using cross-attention to capture pair-specific relationships, while molecule fingerprints and pretrained ESM-2 embeddings provide complementary global information. Compared with state-of-the-art methods, HierDTA achieves superior performance on the Davis data set across all metrics and attains the highestrm2of 0.791 on KIBA. It also exhibits strong generalization under cold-start settings, particularly on KIBA, where MSE is reduced by 21.7% in the unseen-protein scenario. Ablation study and interpretability analysis supported the contributions of the hierarchical augmentation and interaction components. Case studies further showed that HierDTA provided early enrichment of candidate bioactive compounds. These results indicate that HierDTA is an effective framework for affinity prediction and target-specific virtual screening.

item.title: Effects of Hydroponic Barley Green Fodder Supplementation on Egg Quality and Proximate Composition in ATAK-S, Lohmann Brown, and Leghorn Laying Hens
item.description:
Abstract
Hydroponic barley green fodder (HBGF) is increasingly discussed as a low-input, locally producible feed resource for poultry. This study examined how HBGF supplementation affects egg quality traits and the proximate composition of egg white and yolk in three laying-hen genotypes (ATAK-S, Lohmann Brown, and Leghorn) over a 42 day feeding period under free-range conditions. Hens of each genotype were allocated to a control group fed a commercial layer diet and to a group receiving the same feed plus fresh HBGF ad libitum. Egg weight, yolk, albumen, and eggshell percentages, eggshell thickness, egg shape index, yolk color, yolk index, albumen index, and Haugh unit were recorded on days 0, 21, and 42, and the dry matter, crude protein, crude fat, and ash contents of egg white and yolk were determined. Genotype was the primary contributor to variation in egg weight, egg shape index, and albumen index on every sampling day, in Haugh unit on days 0 and 21, in yolk percentage from day 21, and in albumen percentage on day 42 (p < 0.05–0.001). ATAK-S hens produced the heaviest eggs, Lohmann Brown hens had the greatest albumen percentage and egg shape index, and both ATAK-S and Leghorn hens had higher yolk percentage compared to Lohmann Brown. Albumen index and Haugh unit were higher in Lohmann Brown and Leghorn compared to ATAK-S. Eggshell thickness, eggshell percentage, yolk color, and yolk index did not differ among genotypes during the feeding period, apart from a genotype effect on yolk index on day 21 only. HBGF supplementation did not change any physical egg quality trait, including yolk color and yolk index, on day 21 or day 42 (p > 0.05). The proximate composition was mainly affected by the egg percentages (white versus yolk), with the yolk possessing significantly higher levels of dry matter, protein, fat, and ash contents compared to the white. HBGF produced compositional alterations that were both genotype and time dependent, with elevated albumen protein in ATAK-S and Lohmann Brown on day 21, increased yolk fat in ATAK-S and Lohmann Brown but decreased yolk fat in Leghorn, and no consistent change in albumen ash; however, these alterations varied among genotypes. Overall, genotype rather than HBGF influenced egg quality; however, HBGF produced slight changes in some compositional characteristics which tend to be genotype-specific rather than general improvements in egg quality.

item.title: Diosmetin as a Promising Anticancer Agent: Mechanisms, Structural Optimization, and Advanced Delivery Systems
item.description:
Abstract
Diosmetin (Dio) is a natural flavonoid with broad-spectrum anticancer activity against various malignancies through mechanisms involving cell cycle arrest, apoptosis induction, metastasis inhibition, and modulation of oncogenic signaling pathways such as STAT3/c-Myc and PI3K/AKT/mTOR; with the exception of CDK2, which has been proposed as a direct target in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, no other direct molecular targets of diosmetin have been identified to date. It also exhibits synergistic efficacy with reduced toxicity when combined with radiotherapy or chemotherapy. However, clinical translation is severely hampered by poor water solubility, low bioavailability, and unidentified direct molecular targets. Structural modifications (esterification, etherification, phosphorylation) and advanced drug delivery systems (SMEDDS, targeted liposomes, composite nanoparticles) offer promising strategies to overcome these limitations. This review provides an integrated framework covering the complete chain from extraction and chemical derivatization to formulation strategies and anticancer mechanisms, with critical analysis of current translational bottlenecks, particularly the disconnect between in vitro and in vivo findings. By integrating chemical optimization with pharmacological mechanisms, this review aims to provide a theoretical foundation to inform and guide future preclinical and translational research on Dio as a potential adjunct to existing cancer therapies. While some of these strategies have been validated in cancer models, others have been demonstrated in noncancer settings and await translation to oncology.

item.title: Solid-State Synthesis of NMC111 and Impact of Impurities on the Electrochemical Performance
item.description:
Abstract
The growing deployment of electric vehicles will soon generate large quantities of end-of-life Li-ion batteries, making the recovery of Ni–Mn–Co (NMC) cathode active materials critical. Recycling processes often yield individual metal salts that can be directly recombined into NMC through solid-state synthesis, a simple, water-free alternative to coprecipitation. However, recycled precursors may contain residual impurities whose impact on solid-state NMC synthesis remains poorly understood, notably in terms of electrochemical performance. Therefore, investigating the influence of controlled amounts of CuO and/or Na2SO4 (typical residues from battery wastes and hydrometallurgical steps) on the morphology, structure, and electrochemical performance of NMC111 synthesized from carbonate precursors is needed. We report that both impurities reduce particle size and increase the lattice parameters, indicating their partial incorporation into the oxide structure. Cu-containing samples exhibit Cu-rich inclusions, while Na2SO4 induces strong chemical heterogeneity within particles. These impurity-driven microstructural changes enhance high-rate capability but deteriorate cycling stability. Na2SO4-containing materials in particular show rapid capacity fading, whereas low CuO levels (1–2 wt %) maintain chemical homogeneity and deliver aging performances comparable to pristine NMC. This study demonstrates that impurities introduced during solid-state synthesis can hinder particle growth and chemical homogenization, thereby governing the performance of recycled NMC materials.

item.title: Ultrahigh-Capacity Adsorption of Cationic Dyes with Rapid Kinetics Using Used Cigarette Filters-Based Carbons Activated by KHCO 3
item.description:
Abstract
The development of adsorbents that simultaneously achieve high adsorption capacity and rapid kinetics is critical for treating organic dyes, particularly at high concentrations. Herein, novel used cigarette filter (UCF)-based carbons were synthesized via one-step pyrolysis employing an eco-friendly activator KHCO3. The resulting CPCHK-800 carbon material possesses a high specific surface area of 1533 m2/g and a high volume of 0.716 cm3/g. Benefiting from a three-dimensional (3D) honeycomb architecture of graphene-like nanosheets and abundant oxygen groups (19.98 wt %), CPCHK-800 exhibited high adsorption capacities for MB (1328.7 mg/g), RhB (3129.5 mg/g), and MG (3425.9 mg/g) at an adsorbent dosage of 0.2 g/L. Notably, near-complete removal of MB was achieved within 10 min at 100 mg/L, and an adsorption capacity of 1023.9 mg/g was reached within 5 min at 400 mg/L and 0.2 g/L dosage. Such rapid kinetics highlight its potential for treating high-concentration dye wastewater. The Langmuir model best describes the isotherms (R2 = 0.982, qmax = 1657.4 mg/g) with favorable RL values (0.0049–0.0312). The adsorption process is spontaneous and endothermic. Mechanistic studies reveal that MB adsorption involves synergistic contributions from pore filling, hydrogen bonding, electrostatic attraction, π-π, and n-π interactions. Furthermore, CPCHK-800 maintains 92.2% of its initial adsorption capacity after five cycles, decreasing from 1089.3 to 1004.7 mg/g, and maintains 87.3% of its salt-free performance at 0.5 mol/L NaCl, highlighting its excellent reusability and anti-interference capability. These quantitative results confirm that CPCHK-800 is a promising, cost-effective, and environmentally safe adsorbent for practical high-concentration cationic dye wastewater treatment.

item.title: DFT Study on Reactivity and Enantioselectivity in Isothiourea-Catalyzed Synthesis of N–N Atropisomeric N-Aminoindoles
item.description:
Abstract
While N–N atropisomeric N-aminoindoles are prevalent in natural products and bioactive molecules, the origin of reactivity and enantioselectivity in their isothiourea-catalyzed synthesis remains unclear. Herein, density functional theory (DFT) calculations are performed to investigate the mechanism of the isothiourea-catalyzed asymmetric synthesis of N–N atropisomeric N-aminoindoles. Our computational results demonstrate that the catalyst-free pathway proceeds via a high-energy barrier (30.0 kcal/mol) with negligible enantioselectivity. In the presence of the chiral isothiourea catalyst, the calculated energy difference between the two diastereomeric transition states is 4.7 kcal/mol, rationalizing the experimentally observed high enantioselectivity (>99:1 er). Both π–π stacking and nO → σ*S–C delocalization contribute to the stabilization of the rate-determining transition state. Meanwhile, energy decomposition and distortion/interaction analyses reveal that enhanced orbital overlap in the stereoselectivity-determining step governs enantioselectivity. Selenium substitution further lowers the rate-determining barrier from 18.0 to 15.1 kcal/mol without compromising enantioselectivity. In contrast, the NHC catalyst leads to poor chiral discrimination, with an energy difference of only 0.4 kcal/mol, consistent with the experimentally observed 50:50 product ratio. This work elucidates the mechanism of the isothiourea-catalyzed atroposelective synthesis and serves as a guide for the rational design of improved catalysts.

item.title: Constructing an Ohmic-like Type-I Heterojunction via Electrostatic Self-Assembly of Silver Cyanamide and g-C 3 N 4 for Boosted Photocatalytic Performance
item.description:
Abstract
Developing efficient heterojunction photocatalysts for organic pollutant removal remains an important goal in water treatment. We prepared Ag2NCN/g-C3N4 (ACN) composites with different Ag2NCN loadings via electrostatic self-assembly. Under full-spectrum light, ACN-2 degraded 99 % of Rhodamine B within 30 min, with a rate constant 5.7 times that of pristine g-C3N4. It also exhibited good reusability and achieved 61.2 % total organic carbon removal. Mechanistic studies indicated that the composite forms an ohmic-like type-I heterojunction. The Fermi-level offset across the Ag2NCN/g-C3N4 heterojunction gives rise to a built-in electric field at the heterointerface, which facilitates directional charge migration from g-C3N4 toward Ag2NCN and effectively curbs carrier recombination. Superoxide anions (•O2–) and photoinduced holes (h+) served as the dominant reactive species. This work offers a straightforward route to type-I heterojunctions with improved charge separation through interfacial electric field engineering, and provides practical insights for designing effective photocatalysts for wastewater treatment.

item.title: Smart Simulation Solutions for Hybrid Solar Engine Performance
item.description:
Abstract
This work presents the development and validation of a lightweight process simulator capable of reproducing the behavior of a solar-hybrid engine by integrating four computational modules: photovoltaic energy generation, electrochemical energy storage, engine energy supply, and engine operation. The models are solved using a first-order Euler discretization across multiple operating scenarios representative of real hybrid-engine control modes. Model parameters were obtained through time-series fitting of local environmental data, adjustment of solar-panel performance using manufacturer specifications, and targeted experiments isolating the behavior of each subsystem. The simulator accurately reproduced the performance of two hybrid-engine prototypes, an agricultural irrigation system, and an automotive test platform, with correlation coefficients of approximately 0.981 for energy-related variables and 0.926 for chemical species concentrations. The strong agreement between predicted and experimental results demonstrates the robustness of the modeling approach and supports its potential application as an energy-management tool for future solar-hybrid engine systems. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first model in which a chloralkaline process is integrated with solar photovoltaic panels for H2 production and applied in two different scenarios, with the addition of carbon capture within the same procedure.

item.title: Synthesis of Atomically Precise Pt 1 Ag 34 Bimetallic Nanoclusters and Their Catalytic Performance in the Thermal Decomposition of Ammonium Perchlorate
item.description:
Abstract
Exploring the potential applications of metal nanoclusters is of great significance. In this study, we synthesized and characterized Pt1Ag34(C21H21O3P)8(C6F5S)24 (Pt1Ag34) nanocluster by single-crystal X-ray diffraction, which was capped by mercaptans and phosphine ligands. We applied Pt1Ag34 to the thermal decomposition of ammonium perchlorate (AP) and characterized by thermogravimetric-differential scanning calorimetry. The results demonstrate that Pt1Ag34 nanoclusters can significantly reduce the high-temperature thermal decomposition peak of AP by about 100 °C, effectively lowering the activation energy of the reaction. So, we have enriched the structural library of nanoclusters, which holds considerable application prospects in the field of energetic materials for catalytic solid propellants.

item.title: Supramolecular Halogen-Bonded Organic Frameworks (XOFs): From Structural Construction to Functional Applications
item.description:
Abstract
Supramolecular halogen-bonded organic frameworks (XOFs) have emerged as a distinct class of crystalline material in which halogen bonding, rather than covalent or coordination chemistry, defines the framework. Two types of XOFs have developed. Classical XOFs are assembled from electroneutral R–X···D contacts; their single-point character biases assembly toward chains, sheets, and three-dimensional networks. Cationic XOFs exploit halonium ions, whose vacant p orbital bridges two Lewis bases in a three-center, four-electron [N···X···N]+ motif. The halogen scope has widened from iodine(I) through bromine(I) to chlorine(I), a species otherwise observable only transiently at cryogenic temperatures. This review surveys both families with respect to structural classification, synthetic strategy─from cocrystallization to silver–halogen exchange, and dynamic ligand exchange─and functional application, including gas adsorption and separation, iodine capture, photocatalysis, luminescent and vapochromic sensing, and biomedicine. Halogen bonding offers an assembly logic tunable through halogen identity, counterion, and ligand that has no direct analogue in coordination or covalent chemistry.

item.title: Enzymatic Bio-Oxidation of Ethyl Hydroxyethyl Cellulose and UV-Assisted Cross-Linking with Chitosan for Enhanced Aqueous Stability in Biomaterial Production
item.description:
Abstract
Ethyl hydroxyethyl cellulose (EHEC) is a promising sustainable biomaterial, but its high hydrophilicity limits its use in moisture-resistant applications. Conventional cross-linking to improve aqueous resistance often requires toxic reagents, organic solvents, or high temperatures. Here, we developed a green cross-linking method by enzymatically oxidizing EHEC with laccase/TEMPO (2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidin-1-oxyl), followed by UV-induced cross-linking with chitosan at room temperature, yielding a robust macromolecular network. The optimal conditions (4 h oxidation, 50 wt % chitosan, 24 h cross-linking) yielded prolonged aqueous-stable films that maintained structural stability for 3–5 months in aqueous media, depending on pH. Compared to purified EHEC, the biomaterial exhibited enhanced thermal behavior, a 44% increase in elastic modulus (775.6 ± 172.8 MPa), reduced hydrophilicity (75.2 ± 0.7° contact angle, compared to 56.5 ± 0.6° from the original EHEC film), and no release of toxic compounds in cytotoxic assays with L929 fibroblast cells. This methodology is tunable and efficiently produces stable, sustainable EHEC-based films, demonstrating significant promise for advanced aqueous applications and active-ingredient encapsulation.

item.title: Potential Health Benefits of Piceatannol-Rich Extracts from Passiflora edulis f. flavicarpa Seeds on Modulating Gene Expressions Related to Fat Metabolism and Muscle Development in C2C12 Myotubes
item.description:
Abstract
Yellow passion fruits are widely cultivated in many countries. Throughout industrial manufacturing operations, seeds are frequently disposed of as byproducts. Passion fruit seeds are an abundant natural source of piceatannol, which is known for its antioxidant properties and its ability to modulate protein turnover. This study investigated the potential benefits of passion fruit (PF) extract from pulp and juice, as well as piceatannol-rich (PIC) extract from passion fruit seeds, on palmitic acid (PA)-induced myosteatosis-related muscle atrophy in C2C12 myotubes at the transcriptional level. The PIC extract yielded 5.1% (w/w) with a piceatannol concentration of 0.37% (w/w). The result showed that the PIC extract was more effective in free radical scavenging than the piceatannol standard. Additionally, the results demonstrated that PA promoted lipid accumulation while impairing the muscle formation and glucose absorption. However, both PF and PIC extracts demonstrated a significant reduction in PA-induced lipid accumulation, accompanied by suppression of diacylglycerol acyltransferase 1 (Dgat1) expression without altering sirtuin 1 (Sirt1) and uncoupling protein 3 (Ucp3). In addition, both extracts tended to enhance the expression of myosin heavy chain 1 (Myh1) and glucose transporter type 4 (GLUT4), while markedly reducing myostatin (Mstn) expression, suggesting improvements in muscle development and glucose uptake. Furthermore, the PIC extract suppressed pancreatic lipase activity, which minimizes spikes in postprandial triglycerides in the blood circulation of rats. These findings emphasize the potential health benefits of PF and PIC extracts in enhancing glucose absorption and inhibiting fat synthesis in C2C12 myotubes, suggesting potential to mitigate lipid accumulation-related muscle development. The promising findings from cell culture suggest further in vivo investigation for studying their physiological relevance to muscle wasting caused by fat accumulation in obesity.

item.title: Cholesterol Reshapes Electroporation Energetics in Phosphatidylcholine Model Membranes
item.description:
Abstract
Cholesterol modulates membrane packing and mechanics, but how concentration reshapes the free-energy landscape from water-defect nucleation to pore expansion remains incompletely resolved. Here, all-atom molecular dynamics, a continuous joint pore coordinate, umbrella sampling under applied potentials, and unbiased direct-field trajectories were combined for a controlled 300 K DMPC/cholesterol series. Across the low-to-medium range, cholesterol increased the characteristic nucleation-region free-energy cost and pore-edge line tension while making metastable pore states shallower; increasing potential lowered hydrated-defect growth costs. Direct-field simulations at composition-specific operational pore-onset potentials separately showed composition-dependent channel timing and pore lifetimes, operationally defined by continuous-water connectivity. Matched DMPC, POPC, and DOPC membranes containing 20 mol % cholesterol showed lipid-dependent responses in nucleation-region profiles, core hydration, charge-density-derived relative electrostatic potentials, and pore structure. The 66 mol % DMPC system defined a distinct high-cholesterol response that departed from lower-concentration trends. Overall, electroporation emerged as a composition- and field-dependent remodeling of the poration landscape, with the matched 20 mol % systems further revealing lipid-dependent responses.

item.title: Microplastics (PP, PE, PS, and PVC) Induce Structural and Functional Changes in Digestive Enzymes: Insights from Spectroscopic Approaches
item.description:
Abstract
Exposure to microplastics (MPs) poses evolving health risks due to their interactions with biological systems; however, their mechanistic effects on digestive enzymes remain incompletely understood. This study employed in vitro structural and functional analyses, utilizing spectroscopic and enzyme inhibition assays, to investigate the impact of various simulated secondary postconsumer microplastics (PC-MPs) at a single concentration (714 μg/mL/day) on digestive enzymes, including α-amylase, pepsin, and pancreatin. Structural analysis was performed in a simulated digestive fluid system, examining fluorescence and circular dichroism (CD) spectra, including fluorophore quantum yield, quenching percentage, amino acid residue changes, aggregation and complex formation, and the percentage of protein secondary structural content. Functional analysis was conducted using enzyme activity inhibition assays. Comparative spectroscopic findings highlighted marked conformational changes and functional disruptions in digestive enzymes. Fluorescence and CD spectra, along with secondary structure analysis, revealed a consistent loss of emission from (Tyr and Trp) amino acid residues and α-helices and β-sheets, indicating potential destabilization. From the observation, it is evident that PP-MPs have a pronounced impact on α-amylase and pepsin, whereas PE-MPs affect the pancreatic enzyme mixtures. On the other hand, functional analysis revealed that PP-MPs strongly inhibited the activities of salivary α-amylase, pepsin, and pancreatic α-amylase, whereas PS-MPs inhibited pancreatic protease. In the present study, the PP-MPs had a substantial effect on salivary α-amylase and pepsin. In the case of PE- and PS-MPs, distinct differences were observed with pancreatin enzyme, possibly due to the mixture of enzymes contained. This study reveals that PC-MPs disrupt the structure of digestive enzymes and impair their activity, raising concerns about digestive health.

item.title: Gold-Enhanced Multielectrode Electrochemical Immunosensor for Rapid Electrochemical Detection of Dengue NS1
item.description:
Abstract
Dengue is one of the most widespread viral diseases in the world, transmitted mainly by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus. In tropical and resource-limited regions, rapid and accurate diagnostic tools are of utmost importance, especially when aiming for effective control, but current detection methods face limitations in sensitivity, specificity, or accessibility. In this work, a multielectrode disposable electrochemical immunosensor was developed for the detection of the nonstructural protein 1 (NS1), an early biomarker of dengue infection. This device presents four fully individual and functional working electrodes modified with gold nanoparticles. This configuration enables replicate measurements and improved reproducibility within a single platform while using minimal sample volume. The electrodeposition of Au nanoparticles was optimized through Design of Experiments approaches, allowing the system to suitably determine the target protein with a specific biorecognition architecture based on antibody–antigen recognition. This biosensor was characterized by morphological and electrochemical techniques, achieving a linear response between 1.0 and 200 ng mL–1 and a limit of detection of 0.34 ng mL–1. Afterward, human serum samples spiked with NS1 showed recovery rates between 96.6% and 115%. All results indicate that the proposed multielectrode immunosensor is a promising, label-free, and portable diagnostic alternative for NS1 determination while maintaining a relatively low cost and simple preparation.

item.title: Machine Learning-Driven Design of Experiments for CO 2 Mineralization of Steel Slag Materials
item.description:
Abstract
The mineralization of CO2 using steel slag represents a promising pathway for simultaneous carbon sequestration and industrial-waste valorization. However, the complex and nonlinear interactions between process variables hinder the identification of the dominant mechanisms and optimal operating conditions. In this study, a hybrid modeling framework integrating artificial neural networks (ANNs) with factorial design analysis was developed to predict and interpret the performance of three key process routes: leaching, direct carbonation, and indirect carbonation. A comprehensive data set compiled from 58 published studies, comprising 171 leaching, 168 direct carbonation, and 22 indirect carbonation experiments, was used to train and validate ANN models. The trained models were subsequently employed to generate a full factorial design (3k), enabling systematic evaluation of parameter significance and interaction effects. The ANN models demonstrated strong predictive capability for leaching and acceptable performance for carbonation processes, with improved accuracy upon inclusion of reaction time, highlighting the importance of kinetic effects. The ANN–factorial analysis suggests that leaching is most strongly associated with feed composition (CaO content) and leaching agent chemistry, while direct carbonation is controlled by reaction kinetics and surface accessibility, with strong interactions between CO2 availability, pretreatment, and time. Indirect-carbonation results, which are based on the smaller data set, suggest dominant associations with solution-phase chemistry, particularly pH, Ca concentration, and precipitation kinetics, with interaction effects playing a critical role in determining carbonation efficiency. Across all processes, chemical and kinetic interactions were found to be more influential than purely physical parameters. The integration of ANN with factorial design enables the creation of a virtual experimental space, allowing comprehensive exploration of complex multivariable systems beyond experimental limitations. Steel slag mineralization exhibits a progressive shift in dominant control mechanisms, from composition-dominated behavior during leaching to coupled composition–gas-supply control during direct carbonation, and finally to solution-phase control during indirect carbonation. Comparison with our previously studied Mg-rich serpentine system further shows that the ANN–factorial framework is transferable across alkaline feedstocks, while the controlling mechanisms remain feedstock-specific: Mg-rich systems are more strongly governed by pretreatment and pH/additive chemistry, whereas steel slag systems are dominated by reactive Ca availability, CO2 supply, and Ca–carbonate precipitation chemistry. These findings provide a screening framework for process optimization and highlight the importance of material-specific modeling in CO2 mineralization technologies.

item.title: Erythrosine–Iron Oxide Nanoemulsions Combining Photodynamic Therapy with Ferroptosis-Mediated Cytotoxicity in Prostate Cancer
item.description:
Abstract
Prostate cancer remains one of the leading causes of cancer-related death among men worldwide. Photodynamic therapy (PDT) has emerged as a promising strategy to enhance conventional treatments, yet its efficacy is often limited by poor solubility, instability, and a lack of targeting of photosensitizers. Here, we report the development of hybrid erythrosine–iron oxide nanoemulsions (MNE/Ery) produced by vacuum-assisted nanoemulsification. The optimized formulation (0.05 mg·mL–1 erythrosine; 0.5 mg·mL–1 maghemite) exhibited a hydrodynamic diameter of ∼100 nm, negative surface charge, and strong retention of the photosensitizer’s spectral profile. The iron oxide nanoparticles (20–30 nm) exhibited efficient magnetic heating potential, reaching 42 °C within 5.5 min under an alternating field (418 kHz, 12 kA·m–1), indicating suitability for future exploration in magnetic hyperthermia applications. While MNE/Ery maintained high biocompatibility toward healthy cells (HDFn and PNT2), it induced a potent light-triggered cytotoxic response in PC-3 prostate cancer cells. Upon irradiation, the platform delivered a robust, dose-dependent therapeutic effect even at conservative fluences, driven by the combination of maghemite-induced oxidative stress (ferroptosis) and erythrosine-mediated ROS generation. These findings position the MNE/Ery system as a promising nanotechnological platform for PDT with an intrinsic iron-mediated chemotherapeutic effect, with additional potential for future magnetic hyperthermia-based applications.

item.title: Natural Products against Human and Veterinary Trichomonads: From In Vitro Activity to Future Therapeutic Perspectives
item.description:
Abstract
Pathogenic trichomonads are flagellated protozoan parasites of the urogenital and digestive tracts of humans and animals. These organisms impose substantial health and economic burdens on the world. Trichomonas vaginalis causes human urogenital trichomoniasis, the most common nonviral sexually transmitted infection worldwide, and has been associated with adverse reproductive outcomes and increased risk of HIV transmission. In animals, Trichomonas gallinae causes avian trichomoniasis, a disease of the upper digestive tract that may impair feeding, compromise survival, and contribute to bird population declines, whereas Tritrichomonas foetus is responsible for bovine trichomoniasis, a major cause of cattle production losses. Despite their importance, therapeutic options remain limited. Human and avian trichomoniasis still rely on 5-nitroimidazoles, but drug resistance and regulatory restrictions have become important concerns, whereas no approved pharmacological treatment is currently available for bovine trichomoniasis, and infected animals are culled. In this context, natural products have emerged as valuable sources of new antitrichomonal agents. This Review summarizes 84 studies published between 2016 and 2026 investigating natural products against T. vaginalis, T. gallinae, and T. foetus, including plant-derived extracts and fractions, essential oils, isolated compounds, microbial metabolites, and nanotechnology-based formulations. Although several products displayed relevant antitrichomonal activity, most evidence remains restricted to in vitro studies, with comparatively few in vivo evaluations and no clinical validation of natural-product-derived candidates for trichomoniasis. Overall, natural products represent a chemically diverse and still underexplored source of antitrichomonal leads, but further validation of their selectivity, pharmacological properties, and in vivo efficacy is required before their therapeutic potential can be established.

item.title: Design and Evaluation of Fluorescent gRNAs for Visibility Improvement in dCas9-Mediated Live-Cell Imaging
item.description:
Abstract
Live-cell nuclear imaging continues to be limited by the number of fluorescent moieties that may be recruited to the DNA locus of interest. Major advances in dCas9-based live-cell imaging have been made using plasmid-based expression systems that integrate many protein fluorophores into the dCas9 fluorescent ribonucleoprotein (fRNP) complex to increase the visibility of the resulting DNA labels. The dependence on exogenous DNA plasmids, however, precludes these strategies from applications where precise control of fRNP presence is necessary or possible plasmid integration into the genome is unacceptable. In this study, we evaluated the capacity for fluorescent guide RNA (gRNA) to improve the visibility of cellular DNA labels during live-cell imaging, bypassing the need for complex fluorescent protein expression and foreign DNA plasmid delivery. Both CRISPR RNA (crRNA) and trans-activating crRNA (tracrRNA) components of the gRNA were modified with terminal cyanine 3 (Cy3) fluorophores before assembly into fRNP, and the impact on the brightness and signal-to-background (SNB) of the resulting DNA labels was evaluated at two different genomic loci: a repeat-rich Chr3 locus and chromosome telomeres. We further explored the visibility of DNA labeled with a “split” fRNP constructed from two individual tracrRNA fragments, rather than the complete 86 nt tracrRNA sequence, in order to reduce the costs and turnaround time of tracrRNA synthesis and to increase the terminal ends available for fluorophore modification. The 86 nt tracrRNA configuration bearing two terminal Cy3 modifications to both the crRNA and tracrRNA resulted in the greatest improvement to label visibility with a 190% increase in brightness and a 60% increase in SNB for both loci, on average, in comparison to the previously published fRNP containing only one Cy3 on the crRNA. The split tracrRNA fRNP was capable of labeling both genomic loci with varying success, imparting a maximum brightness improvement of 153% and an SNB improvement of 49% to Chr3 labeling, however, with no significant gains to brightness and 41% improved SNB for telomeres. For both the designs, label visibility improved consistently with additional fluorescence modification of the gRNA, indicating that the modifications were well tolerated, and further enhancement of gRNA fluorescence may continue to improve label visibility during live-cell imaging.

item.title: Dyeing and Multifunctional Finishing of Cotton Fabrics Using Ethiopian Rumex steudelii Root Extract: Response Surface Optimization, LC-MS/MS Phytochemical Profiling, and Antibacterial and UV-Protective Performance
item.description:
Abstract
Textile finishing increasingly demands sustainable, multifunctional alternatives to synthetic dyes and biocides. This study developed a single-bath, metal-free strategy to simultaneously color and biofunctionalize 100% cotton fabric using Rumex steudelii root extract. Ultrasonic-assisted extraction was optimized by response surface methodology (central composite design, CD); experimental yield ranged from 29.95% to 40.13% across the design space. The desirability-based optimum, selected to minimize temperature, time, and solvent use, was ≈55 °C, 32 min, and a 10 mL/g liquid-to-solid ratio, a predicting yield of 34.51%, which was confirmed experimentally (33.90 ± 0.18%, prediction error 1.77%). LC-MS/MS annotated 27 constituents (24 confirmed with authentic standards), dominated by flavonoids (35.38%), phenolic acids (22.25%), and anthraquinones (19.28%), providing a chemical basis for coupling coloration with bioactivity. Dyeing with the extract alone, or with citric acid or tannic acid as green cross-linkers, produced three distinct, reproducible shades (golden yellow, burnt orange, and earth brown) with color strength (K/S) of 4.42 to 10.34, and washing, rubbing, and light fastness improved to grades of 4/5–5. Cross-linked fabrics achieved excellent UV protection (UPF up to 56) and strong antibacterial activity, reducing Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli counts by up to 99.8 ± 0.23% and 97.3 ± 0.81%, respectively. By integrating RSM-optimized extraction, LC-MS/MS-resolved phytochemical mapping, and single-bath, metal-free cross-linking in one process, this work establishes Rumex steudelii as a promising platform for multifunctional natural textile finishing, with potential for scale-up pending pilot-scale validation.

item.title: Heparin-Binding Proteins in the Nanoparticle Corona: An Overlooked Player at the Bio–Nano Interface
item.description:
Abstract
When nanoparticles (NPs) enter biological environments, they rapidly acquire a layer of adsorbed proteins, known as the protein corona, which plays a central role in their interactions with cells. While extensive work has focused on how corona proteins interact with cell-surface receptors to modulate NP uptake, the role of corona–glycocalyx interactions has received comparatively little attention. In this Minireview, we highlight emerging evidence that heparin-binding proteins (HBPs) within the protein corona can engage glycosaminoglycans, such as heparan sulfate, in the cellular glycocalyx, thereby introducing an additional layer of molecular recognition at the cell surface. Drawing on recently published protein corona data sets, we further show that HBPs are frequently present and often abundant across protein coronas from diverse NP systems. These observations highlight HBPs as important, yet underappreciated, mediators of NP–cell interactions and uptake.

item.title: Novel Trilinear Flow Model for a Fractured Horizontal Well Considering Spatially Linear Decline of Fracture Conductivity
item.description:
Abstract
Pressure transient analysis (PTA) of a fractured horizontal well often relies on a trilinear flow model, but a conventional trilinear flow model assumes uniform fracture conductivity along the whole fracture length and therefore may overestimate the contribution of less-conductive fracture sections. A novel analytical trilinear flow model is proposed in this work for pressure analysis by considering a linearly declining fracture conductivity distribution from the wellbore toward the fracture tip through a new parameter (conductivity decline coefficient). The new trilinear flow problem was analytically solved in the Laplace domain, yielding a closed form solution expressed with modified Bessel functions; asymptotic limits were derived to ensure numerical stability without discretizing the fracture into multiple segments. The proposed model has been validated by comparing its results with those of the traditional trilinear flow model with uniform fracture conductivity. It is found that the conductivity decline coefficient mainly affects the middle-time transient pressure behavior by increasing the pressure and pressure derivative. Sensitivity results for CfD0 = 10 and 50 show that a decline coefficient with 1 can elevate the middle-time pressure and pressure derivative by up to 13% and 14%, respectively. The maximum fracture conductivity controls the early time pressure response, whereas well spacing and fracture spacing primarily determine the onset of late-time boundary-dominated flow. In dual-porosity SRV systems, the storativity ratio and interporosity-flow coefficient govern the timing and depth of the concave pressure derivative signature. The proposed model can provide a fast and physically interpretable PTA tool for estimating fracture/reservoir parameters, evaluating conductivity degradation, predicting production performance, and assessing spacing-controlled boundary interaction in fractured tight reservoirs.

item.title: Comparison of Alkane Distributions in Crude Oils Detected by Gas Chromatography of Whole Oils and Saturated Fractions and Gas Chromatography–Mass Spectrometry of Saturated Fractions
item.description:
Abstract
Alkane-related parameters of oils obtained by both gas chromatography (GC) and gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC-MS) were widely used in oil-source correlation. However, it is still unclear whether different detection methods will lead to significant differences in these parameters. The compositions of alkanes in Jurassic oils from the Sichuan Basin were investigated using GC analysis of whole-oil samples and saturated hydrocarbons and GC-MS analysis of saturated hydrocarbons. Comparative analyses of alkane-related parameters obtained by these detection methods were also performed in this study. n-Alkanes in the range nC3–nC35 were detected in oils using whole-oil GC analysis. By contrast, short-chain n-alkanes (nC3–nC13) were not detected by GC and GC-MS analysis of saturated hydrocarbons. The abundances of n-alkanes in the range nC14–nC16 were lower than those detected by whole-oil GC analysis. nC21–/nC22+ ratios and terrigenous/aquatic ratios (TAR = (nC27 + nC29 + nC31)/(nC15 + nC17 + nC19)) obtained by GC analysis of saturated hydrocarbons are similar to those obtained by m/z 85 mass chromatograms of GC-MS and show huge differences from those obtained by whole-oil GC analysis and total ion current of GC-MS. However, the differences between these ratios obtained by GC analysis of saturated hydrocarbons, m/z 85 mass chromatograms, and total ion current of GC-MS are systematic. Pristane/phytane (Pr/Ph) ratios obtained by GC analysis of saturated hydrocarbons exhibit little difference from those obtained by total ion current of GC-MS but show large differences from those obtained by whole-oil GC and m/z 85 mass chromatograms of GC-MS. While, the differences between Pr/Ph obtained by all these methods mentioned above are systematic and can be basically eliminated. Additionally, the different detection methods have no influence on carbon preference index, odd-to-even preference, Pr/nC17 and Ph/nC18.

item.title: Multi-Enzyme Peptide Mapping of Site-Selective Trastuzumab Modification by an Engineered Thermostable Microbial Transglutaminase
item.description:
Abstract
Peptide mapping by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) is a key analytical strategy for residue-level characterization of antibody conjugates, providing modification-site assignments and apparent relative modification estimates that complement intact-mass and chromatographic drug-to-antibody ratio (DAR) measurements. The development of homogeneous antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) relies on precise control of the conjugation site and DAR. For site-selectively modified ADCs, in which amino acid-level homogeneity is an important quality attribute, peptide mapping is therefore not only a confirmatory assay but also a central component of structural characterization. However, its reliability depends on enzymatic coverage and sample-handling conditions that affect the recovery of hydrophobic Fc-derived peptides, particularly in conjugates generated at high modification levels. In this study, we evaluated a multi-enzyme LC–MS/MS peptide-mapping workflow for antibody conjugates generated by microbial transglutaminase (MTG)-mediated Fc modification, using trastuzumab conjugated with dansylcadaverine (DNC) as a model system. An engineered thermostable MTG variant carrying five amino acid substitutions (D3C/S101P/G157S/G250R/G283C) was used to prepare a highly modified trastuzumab-DNC conjugate for evaluation of complementary protease coverage, residue-level modification-site assignment, and recovery of hydrophobic Fc-derived peptides. The engineered MTG was also compared with the commercial MTG formulation Activa using glycosylated trastuzumab under the specified nominal enzyme-loading conditions. Because this comparison was not normalized on the basis of catalytic activity under the antibody-conjugation conditions, it was treated as a formulation-based reference and was not used to establish intrinsic superiority of either enzyme preparation. Complementary digestion with trypsin, chymotrypsin, and Glu-C provided convergent evidence that DNC modification was predominantly localized to heavy-chain Q298 and enabled evaluation of other detectable glutamine-containing peptides. We further found that post-digestion addition of guanidine hydrochloride (GnHCl) during quenching increased the recovery of hydrophobic Fc-derived peptides, most notably the Q298-containing peptides. Omission of GnHCl during quenching reduced the recovery of several hydrophobic Fc-derived peptides and could bias peptide-map-based apparent modification estimates under the tested conditions. Under the optimized workflow, Q298 consistently showed the highest peptide-map-based apparent modification level, whereas apparent modification levels at other unambiguously assigned glutamine residues remained low under the tested conditions. However, these peak-area-based values do not represent absolute molar occupancy, and low-abundance off-site modifications below the analytical detection threshold cannot be excluded. These findings demonstrate that multi-enzyme peptide mapping combined with denaturant-assisted quenching provides a practical analytical workflow for residue-level characterization of highly modified, site-selective antibody conjugates. The workflow supports predominant modification at heavy-chain Q298 under the tested conditions and highlights the importance of sample-preparation optimization in peptide mapping-based characterization of ADCs and related antibody conjugates. Because DNC is a model primary amine, application of this workflow to therapeutic ADC linker-payloads will require substrate-specific optimization and analytical qualification.

item.title: One-Pot Synthesis of Pt–Fe for EOR: Effect of pH
item.description:
Abstract
The development of efficient electrocatalysts for the ethanol oxidation reaction (EOR) remains a major challenge for direct ethanol fuel cells (DEFCs) due to slow kinetics and catalyst poisoning by reaction intermediates. Herein, Pt/C and Pt–Fe/C catalysts were prepared via a one-pot polyol synthesis, and the effect of pH on Fe incorporation and catalytic performance was investigated. X-ray diffraction showed lattice contraction in Pt–Fe catalysts, confirming Fe incorporation, which was more pronounced under alkaline conditions. Electrochemical measurements demonstrated a strong dependence on both Fe addition and pH. Pt–Fe/C at pH 11.4 achieved a mass activity density of 850 A/gPt, outperforming not only Pt–Fe/C neutral and Pt/C but also the commercial Pt/C catalyst at 20 mV/s. Moreover, a lower onset potential (0.479 V) and a higher If/Ib ratio (1.9) indicate faster reaction kinetics and qualitatively suggest tolerance to adsorbed intermediates. The enhanced performance is attributed to the synergistic effect of Fe incorporation through electronic and bifunctional mechanisms.

item.title: Mechanism and Application of Imidazolium Derivatives as a Bifunctional Additive for Void-free Blind via Copper Filling
item.description:
Abstract
In conventional acidic copper electroplating, the accelerator and leveler are typically provided by different molecules, resulting in complex additive formulations and difficult-to-control intermolecular interactions. This study proposes an “intramolecular functional group division” strategy and designs a series of imidazolium salts bearing different substituents as bifunctional additives, integrating the leveling function of the imidazolium cation and the accelerating function of the pendant groups within a single molecule. Electrochemical measurements, electroplating of silicon-based micro blind vias, and multi-scale characterization demonstrate that a simplified binary system consisting solely of this additive and PEG8000 can achieve void-free superconformal filling. Systematic comparison of four imidazole derivatives containing sulfonate, cyano, and carboxyl substituents establishes a clear structure–activity relationship: the sulfonate group is the key moiety that confers the accelerating effect, Cl– bridging is a prerequisite for strong adsorption, and the structural basis for acceleration is that the sulfonate group remains exposed on the outer surface without participating in copper-surface adsorption. DFT calculations further elucidate this mechanism from the perspectives of electronic structure and adsorption configuration. This work elevates the integration of dual functions in copper electroplating additives from intermolecular synergy to the single-molecule level, providing a new paradigm for the design of multifunctional electroplating additives.

item.title: Cytoplasmic Expression of Papain Isozymes in Engineered Escherichia coli for Substrate Selectivity and Computational Insights
item.description:
Abstract
Challenges in isolating individual papain isozymes from papaya latex and in producing full-length, correctly folded, and soluble recombinant papain isozymes in Escherichia coli have limited detailed investigations into their distinct enzymatic properties and substrate specificities. In this study, we report the successful high-yield cytoplasmic expression of papain, protease omega, proteinase IV (pro-IV), and chymopapains I, II, and III in engineered E. coli SHuffle strains and a comprehensive investigation of their distinct biochemical and computational mechanistic insights. Building upon our previous work, we employed an engineered SHuffle strain using two synthetic constructs. In the first, each isozyme is translationally fused with maltose-binding protein (MBP) and expressed under engineered T7 promoters. In the second, each isozyme was co-expressed with thiol peroxidase glutathione peroxidase-7 (GPx7), and protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) pairs, yielding ∼349 mg/L soluble recombinant papain. We then hypothesized that by using this strain with the above two synthetic constructs, each isozyme would be successfully expressed as soluble proteases. Indeed, the engineered E. coli SHuffle strain produced purified papain and isozymes in yields ranging from 340 to 355 mg/L in batch fermentation. Each isozyme was kinetically characterized using two synthetic substrates, benzyloxycarbonyl-Phe-Arg-pNA and acetyl-Phe-Gly-pNA, revealing catalytic efficiencies spanning from 9.4 × 102 to 2.52 × 105 M–1 s–1 and marked differences in substrate selectivity. The optimum temperature, pH activity profiles, thermostability, and responses to metal ions were determined, revealing significant functional diversity. Structural modeling and docking studies were carried out, revealing nonconserved residues in proteinase IV that distort the active-site geometry. Site-directed mutagenesis of the conserved residues (E23G/R65G) in proteinase IV improved its catalytic function, demonstrating that active-site remodeling contributes to enhanced proteolytic activity.
