This finding is notable because EMPA was previously established as a predictor of mesothelial carcinogenicity. Combining SZ and another coefficient with toxicological implications (Dimensional Coefficient of Carcinogenicity or DCC) provides the effective discrimination of particles as asbestiform or nonasbestiform, yielding a 0% error rate with an upper bound of 14.7%. In vitro study demonstrated that the viability of human mesothelial cells exposed to elongate mineral particles is increasing with their surface roughness and decreasing with iron content. Additionally, the machine learning approach using a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) successfully distinguished asbestiform fibers from cleavage fragments via AFM image processing. Future studies are needed to elucidate the full toxicological mechanisms by which surface roughness impacts the predicted habit and carcinogenicity of elongate mineral particles.

item.title: Microenvironmental-Regulated Chondroitin Sulfate Nanomicelles for Inhibition of Breast Cancer Drug Resistance and Metastasis
item.description:
Abstract
Tumor microenvironment is closely involved in breast cancer progression and metastatic spread. Therefore, it is essential to develop a combination therapy to suppress tumor progression by regulating TME. Herein, Ru486-loaded doxorubicin (DOX)–chondroitin sulfate (chondroitin sulfate) nanomicelles (R/D-CS) were prepared for combined delivery. A “MCF-7 + MRC-5” dual-cell model and “4T1 + NIH-3T3” cell-bearing mouse model were established to recapitulate TME in vitro and in vivo, respectively. Interestingly, R/D-CS nanomicelles internalized cancer-associated fibroblasts and tumor cells and reduced tumor proliferation and migration markedly by downregulating expression of P-gp, vimentin, and CXCR4. Moreover, the in vivo antitumor studies were performed on a tumor-bearing mouse model, R/D-CS nanomicelles showed stronger antiproliferative and antimetastatic effects. Overall, the combination therapy based on R/D-CS nanomicelles was potent for breast cancer treatment.

item.title: Tailoring Fusion Proteins for Interfacial Nanoparticle Functionalization: Toward Fluorescence-Guided Imaging
item.description:
Abstract
Fusion proteins are specially designed molecules created by linking two or more peptides that were originally encoded by separate DNA sequences. To improve control of protein adsorption on poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) (PHB) surfaces, we developed fusion proteins comprising a polyester substrate-binding domain (SBD) fused to superfolder green fluorescent protein (sfGFP). The subunits were connected via flexible (GGGGS)n or rigid (EAAAK)n linkers with n = 1, 2, or 4. The PHB immobilization efficiency provided by these fusion proteins was extensively evaluated on microparticles and nanoparticles by using various surface-sensitive techniques. Accordingly, constructs linked by rigid sequences with n = 2 and n = 4 exhibited higher PHB adsorption capability. This suggests that reduced interdomain conformational freedom may favor configurations compatible with SBD-mediated interaction with the PHB interface. The stable association of the constructs with PHB nanoparticles enabled fluorescence-based tracking during cellular uptake experiments. The spatial orientation and polyester-binding ability conferred by such constructs via a facile, mild, and persistent association process might represent a significant biotechnological advance in the development of advanced nanosystems sensitive to fluorescence imaging.

item.title: Mechanistic Divergence and Ozone Mass Transfer Enhancement in Photocatalytic Ozonation: A Comparative Study of Bimetallic Pd/Cu-Modified Rutile TiO 2 and g-C 3 N 4
item.description:
Abstract
Beyond conventional removal-efficiency metrics, this investigation reveals a mechanistic divergence between two prominent photocatalysts in ozone activation. Both (Pd/Cu) bimetallic g-C3N4 and rutile TiO2 enable efficient antibiotic degradation and antibiotic resistance genes inactivation; however, they rely on fundamentally different reaction pathways. (Pd/Cu)1%C3N4 predominantly generates reactive oxygen species (ROS), including singlet oxygen (1O2) and superoxide radical anion (O2●–), whereas (Pd/Cu)1%TiO2 targets specific sequences like intl1 bypassing conventional ROS pathways. In addition, our research highlights a critical design trade-off and operational paradox in advanced oxidation processes: while a low bimetallic loading (0.1 wt %) optimizes the initial chemical degradation kinetics of both antibiotics and antibiotic resistance genes during active treatment, a higher loading (1.0 wt %) is strictly indispensable for suppressing long-term bacterial regrowth and preventing the biological resuscitation of resistance markers during post-treatment storage. Moreover, this study challenges conventional methodological paradigms by demonstrating that diagnostic scavengers are not inert probes but reactive species that accelerate ozone (O3) depletion and alter mass-transfer behavior, potentially confounding mechanistic interpretations. In complex wastewater matrices dominated by dissolved organic matter, such competitive interactions necessitate rigorous scavenger validation to ensure reliable translation of laboratory findings to scalable purification systems.

item.title: The Role of BaCO 3 on Ni-BaZrO 3 Catalysts for Efficient NH 3 Decomposition
item.description:
Abstract
Barium zirconate (BaZrO3) is a versatile material that has recently gained attention as a catalyst support for ammonia decomposition. In this study, an innovative synthesis strategy for BaZrO3 is combined with a solvent-free dry-milling method to deposit nickel onto its surface. The resulting Ni-BaZrO3 catalyst exhibited superior performance in ammonia decomposition for COx-free hydrogen production, outperforming both traditionally synthesized BaZrO3-based systems and more conventional Ni-supported catalysts. Comprehensive material characterization─using XRD, N2 adsorption–desorption, ATR, and Raman spectroscopy─confirmed that the new synthesis route improves the structural and chemical properties of the perovskite compared to conventional methods. H2-TPR and CO2-TPD analyses revealed that exploiting superficial BaCO3 reduction to BaO enhanced surface defectivity, and a high density of basic sites interacting with Ni nanoparticles can be obtained, facilitating electron exchange between the support and the metal. The mechanism of BaO formation and interaction with CO2 in TPD was deeply analyzed using in situ characterization techniques. Further mechanistic insights into product formation and release were obtained via TPSR and DRIFTS, emphasizing the critical role of metal-support interaction through the formation of Ni-BaO entities on the catalyst surface. Overall, this work demonstrates a sustainable and scalable route for producing high-performance Ni-BaZrO3 catalysts and advances the understanding of their reactivity, focusing on the importance of the metal-support interplay and reinforcing their potential in green hydrogen production through ammonia decomposition.

item.title: A Smartphone-Assisted Schirmer Strip for Rapid Dual Colorimetric Sensing of Tear Glucose and pH Level
item.description:
Abstract
Although tear biomarkers are routinely determined using various clinical methods, most current techniques are complex, time-consuming, and require expensive equipment. Therefore, point-of-care (POC) testing is attracting considerable attention for rapid and noninvasive analyses. Here, we present a dual-function colorimetric Schirmer strip for the simultaneous determination of tear glucose and pH using the naked eye and image processing software. In our approach, horseradish peroxidase-glucose oxidase nanoflowers (HRP–GOx@NF) are used for glucose detection, and red cabbage-derived anthocyanins are used as a pH-sensitive, nontoxic indicator. In glucose detection, the catalytic stepwise reaction of HRP–GOx@NF produced a distinct blue color within 30 s by enabling the rapid oxidation of 3,3′,5,5′-tetramethylbenzidine (TMB) in the presence of glucose, and this optimized platform exhibited a visual detection limit of 0.5 mM. Additionally, the anthocyanin-modified Schirmer strip simultaneously displayed distinct color transitions in response to varying pH values of the artificial tear fluid. This work presents a novel multiparametric paper platform that uniquely upgrades standard Schirmer strips for simultaneous, single-step tear collection, glucose sensing, and pH mapping without altering fluid flow. Like this, it demonstrates a rapid, cost-effective, and easy-to-prepare diagnostic tool offering significant advantages over conventional methods.

item.title: [Graphical abstract added] Allosteric Communication in the Tubulin Dimer Revealed through Molecular Dynamics and Network Analysis
Highly Stable PLA/Gelatin Bionanocomposites for Enhanced Delivery of Chloroaluminum Phthalocyanine for Photodynamic Therapy against SK-MEL-28 Cells
item.description:
Abstract
This study reports the development of a biodegradable poly(lactic acid) and gelatin (nPLA-G) bionanocomposite as a drug delivery system for chloroaluminum phthalocyanine (ClAlPc) in photodynamic therapy (PDT). Using a hybrid desolvation/emulsification technique, we engineered spherical nanoparticles with an average diameter of 753.3 nm and a positive zeta potential of +8.90 mV. ClAlPc-loaded nanoparticles (nPLA-G/ClAlPc) were prepared using the same process, with a mean diameter of 809.3 nm and a zeta potential of +16.10 mV. The system achieved an exceptional encapsulation efficiency of 90.89% and maintained colloidal stability for over 270 days. In vitro assays showed a pH-dependent release profile, optimizing drug availability in tumoral microenvironments. The nPLA-G/ClAlPc system showed no dark toxicity but reached 97% cytotoxicity in SK-MEL-28 melanoma cells upon light activation (1.0 μmol L–1). These preliminary results demonstrate that the bionanocomposite effectively overcomes ClAlPc hydrophobicity, serving as a promising drug delivery system with preliminary photodynamic efficacy in vitro.

item.title: Nanostructured Hybrid Matrix Device: An Engineered Approach for Localized Photodynamic Therapy in 9L/lacZ Cell Models
item.description:
Abstract
Gliosarcoma treatment remains a challenge due to its aggressiveness and high recurrence rates. This study describes the development and characterization of a novel hybrid drug delivery system (DDS) for localized photodynamic therapy (PDT). The system consists of a PVA/gelatin hydrogel encapsulated with hydroxyapatite microspheres (meHAp) loaded with chloroaluminum phthalocyanine (ClAlPc). SEM and FTIR analysis confirmed the successful incorporation of meHAp into the porous 3D polymeric network. The addition of meHAp increased the matrix’s structural rigidity, adjusting the swelling degree and enabling a more controlled release of the photosensitizer (45% vs 94% in the control). Biological assays on 9L/lacZ gliosarcoma cells revealed high internalization and a 98% reduction in cell viability under PDT protocols. These results suggest that the meHAp-reinforced hydrogel system is a promising option for the localized treatment of brain tumors, providing a modified release of the photosensitizer.

item.title: The Application of Waste Coal Fly Ash as a Support for a Heterogeneous Catalyst for Biodiesel Production and a Comparison with the Engine Characteristics Using a Homogeneous Catalyst
item.description:
Abstract
Coal fly ash is a waste product of coal-fired boiler combustion. The fly ash consists of fine glass microspheres with a relatively large surface area. This study aims to synthesize catalysts using waste coal fly ash as a support and calcine them with alkaline catalysts. Fly ash with a large surface area was synthesized using sodium methoxide to prepare a heterogeneous catalyst, which was then used to transesterify palm oil to produce biodiesel. Subsequently, engine performance and exhaust emissions from biodiesel combustion were evaluated. The experimental results indicate that biodiesel prepared with the heterogeneous catalyst exhibited lower fuel consumption and brake-specific fuel consumption (BSFC) than biodiesel prepared with the homogeneous catalyst, and it had a higher brake thermal efficiency. The emission concentrations of CO, CO2, and NOX are higher in biodiesel produced with homogeneous catalysts, whereas the O2 emission concentration from biodiesel prepared with a heterogeneous catalyst is lower than that of homogeneous biodiesel. Moreover, the biodiesel produced using a heterogeneous catalyst consisting of coal fly ash containing sodium methoxide appeared to have a lower excess air ratio and heating value, while exhibiting a higher exhaust gas temperature and fuel/air equivalence ratio. Using waste coal fly ash to synthesize a heterogeneous catalyst improves biodiesel properties, thereby advancing the circular economy.

item.title: Comparative Analysis of the Binding Characteristics of Fluorescein and Rhodamine B with Bovine Serum Albumin
item.description:
Abstract
Bovine serum albumin (BSA) serves as a key model for investigating protein–ligand interactions and is crucial for understanding drug pharmacokinetics and developing biomedical probes. This study presents a comprehensive comparative analysis of the binding of fluorescein and rhodamine B to BSA, employing UV–vis absorption, fluorescence, molecular docking, and 1000 ns molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. The results revealed competitive binding, with rhodamine B exhibiting a greater affinity (ΔGMMGBSA = −48.17 kcal/mol) than fluorescein (−23.16 kcal/mol), which was supported by fluorescence quenching and binding analyses. Molecular docking confirmed Sudlow’s site I as the primary binding site, whereas MD simulations highlighted stable complexes driven by van der Waals and electrostatic forces, particularly for rhodamine B. Unexpectedly, the superior affinity of rhodamine B under physiological pH deviates from lipophilic trends. These findings enhance the molecular understanding of dye–protein interactions, providing a robust basis for designing advanced fluorescent probes, drug conjugates, and diagnostic platforms.

item.title: Experimental Investigation of Engine Performance and Emission Characteristics of a Compression Ignition Engine Fueled with Exhaust-Gas-Assisted Preheated Ethanol–Diesel Blends
item.description:
Abstract
Improving the utilization of low-cetane renewable oxygenated fuels without compromising compression ignition (CI) engine efficiency remains a critical challenge. This study addresses this limitation with a self-sustaining thermal management strategy that couples ethanol–diesel blending (E10–E40) with a waste-heat-driven helical coil heat exchanger. By recovering exhaust thermal energy that would otherwise be wasted, the system raises blend temperature to an operational optimum of 40 °C without external power input, directly counteracting ethanol’s high latent heat of vaporization and low cetane number. Experiments on a single-cylinder CI engine across multiple loads show that this thermal conditioning significantly reduces blend viscosity and density, facilitating superior atomization. While ethanol’s lower energy density increased brake-specific fuel consumption (BSFC) by up to 41.94%, the preheating loop stabilized combustion and mitigated the brake thermal efficiency (BTE) deficit. Environmental benefits were most pronounced at high load, with NOx and CO2 emissions decreasing by up to 11.43% and 20%, respectively. The E20–D80 blend preheated to 40 °C provided the most robust balance between mechanical performance and emission reduction, with one-way ANOVA and uncertainty analysis confirming the statistical reliability of the measured trends. These findings establish waste-heat recovery as a practical, hardware-ready pathway for expanding the operational limits of alcohol-based fuels in conventional CI engines.

item.title: Exploring Bacteria from Extreme Environments in Chilean Patagonia for Antitrypanosomal Metabolites
item.description:
Abstract
Extreme environments are recognized as valuable reservoirs of microbial diversity and chemical novelty. Adapted to harsh environmental conditions, bacteria isolated from extreme environments exhibit unique biosynthetic capabilities associated with the production of structurally diverse bioactive metabolites. Chagas disease (CD), caused by the protozoan parasite Trypanosoma cruzi, remains one of the most important neglected tropical diseases, affecting approximately eight million people worldwide. Current chemotherapy relies on only two drugs, benznidazole and nifurtimox, both associated with toxicity and therapeutic limitations. The search for new antitrypanosomal agents has therefore intensified, directing attention to underexplored microbial resources such as bacteria isolated from extreme environments, which are known for their remarkable biosynthetic potential and chemical diversity. In this context, the present study investigated the anti-T. cruzi potential of extracts obtained from sediment-associated microbial communities from the Magallanes Region of Chilean Patagonia. By using 16S rRNA sequencing, seven bacterial isolates from extreme environments were identified as belonging to the genus Roseovarius spp., Loktanella spp., Pseudarthrobacter spp., Pseudomonas spp., Psychroflexus spp., and Cyclobacterium spp. The antiparasitic activity of the extracts was determined in trypomastigotes, resulting in potent IC50 values ranging from 2 to 18 μg/mL. Bioactivity-guided fractionation of the Cyclobacterium plantarum extract led to the putative identification of VAS8, a phosphatidylethanolamine derivative, as its active constituent. VAS8 exhibited activity against both trypomastigote (IC50 = 49 μM) and intracellular amastigote (IC50 = 19 μM) forms of T. cruzi, while showing no significant cytotoxicity toward mammalian host cells (CC50 > 150 μM). Spectrofluorimetric and fluorescence microscopy studies using SYTOX Green demonstrated a time/concentration-dependent permeabilization of the plasma membrane after VAS8 incubation with trypomastigotes. These findings highlight bacteria isolated from extreme environments as a promising source of antitrypanosomal metabolites and phosphatidylethanolamines as attractive scaffolds for the development of new therapies against Chagas disease.

item.title: Discovery of a Peripherally Directed CB 1 Receptor Antagonist That Restores Insulin Signaling in Adipocytes
item.description:
Abstract
The antagonism of cannabinoid 1 receptor (CB1R) signaling has demonstrated clinical efficacy in treating obesity, improving insulin resistance, enhancing cardiovascular health, and mitigating metabolic risk factors in humans. Despite these positive outcomes, the clinical use of rimonabant was limited by severe central nervous system adverse effects, which reduced interest in CB1R and hindered the exploration of new therapeutic opportunities. Selective targeting of peripheral CB1R represents a promising strategy to overcome these limitations, creating therapeutic opportunities not only for obesity and metabolic disorders but also for smoking and alcohol addiction. Herein, we report a library of 53 novel, potent, and subtype-selective CB1R antagonists bearing polar groups, designed through convergent Ugi-based synthetic pathways. This approach enabled the identification of key structure–activity relationship features within this series and the effective modulation of molecular properties governing blood–brain barrier permeability. Among the compounds evaluated, the piperazine-1-ium derivative 24a stands out as the first permanently charged CB1R antagonist, exhibiting nanomolar affinity (Ki = 115 nM) and high CB1R/CB2R selectivity with a favorable physicochemical profile consistent with peripheral restriction and limited blood-brain barrier penetration. Importantly, 24a exhibits robust functional activity in a biologically relevant model of metabolic dysfunction. In insulin-resistant, lipid-hypertrophied adipocytes, 24a restores insulin-stimulated Akt phosphorylation and significantly enhances lipolytic activity, with effects comparable or superior to those of rimonabant at equivalent concentrations. These findings establish 24a as a promising peripherally restricted CB1R antagonist with demonstrated functional efficacy in a metabolic disease-relevant cellular model.

item.title: Elucidating the Action Mechanism of the Carbon Substrate in Pt/C-Catalyzed Alkaline Hydrogen Evolution Reaction
item.description:
Abstract
In the alkaline hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), loading Pt on a carbon substrate can markedly enhance its activity. Electrochemical tests show that the Tafel slopes of Pt/C and Pt mesh are 73 and 171 mV dec–1, respectively, which indicate the HER mechanisms on Pt/C and Pt are different. In alkaline media, the HER on Pt is limited by H2O dissociation. Therefore, in this paper, the effect of the carbon substrate on the H2O dissociation process on a Pt cluster was systematically studied by density functional theory (DFT) calculations. The results indicate that the electron redistribution of the Pt cluster caused by the carbon substrate can enhance the Lewis acidity of the active site, thereby accelerating H2O dissociation step on the Pt cluster. Therefore, promoting the H2O dissociation step on Pt by the carbon substrate is one of the prime reasons for the eminent activity of Pt/C in the alkaline HER.

item.title: Detection of Neonicotinoid-Contaminated Drinking Water by D-SERS and SIMCA Class Modeling
item.description:
Abstract
Neonicotinoids are insecticides widely used in agriculture and are highly toxic to invertebrates. There is evidence linking the use of neonicotinoids to declines in bee populations. Due to their high persistence, these compounds can remain in soil and water for long periods and are frequently detected in surface water, groundwater, and even drinking water, thereby posing risks to human health. This study reports the development of a polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE)-based AgNP substrate for the detection of the neonicotinoids imidacloprid (IMD), thiamethoxam (THX), and their mixture in drinking water using the D-SERS (Dynamic-Surface Enhancement Raman Spectroscopy) methodology, together with the development of a class-modeling method based on Soft Independent Modeling of Class Analogy (SIMCA) that allowed the classification of drinking water samples containing one or more pesticides, achieving an efficiency of 97%. This study presents the first reported application of the SIMCA model for the classification of neonicotinoids.

item.title: Influence of Crude Oil Production Chemicals on the Stability of O/A Emulsions and on Flocculant Efficiency
item.description:
Abstract
The water produced during oil extraction contains oil emulsified. Therefore, before being reinjected or discarded, this produced water must comply with the oil in water concentration limits established by Brazil’s environmental regulatory authority, CONAMA. These limits correspond to a monthly average of 29 mg/L and a maximum daily value of 42 mg/L. Treatment of the emulsified fraction, one the most resistant to separation, is commonly carried out flocculation with water-soluble polymers. In this work, synthetic oily waters using heavy oil were prepared, and two types of cationic polymeric flocculants were evaluated, both individually and in combination with a commercial demulsifier and an anionic SPAM polymer, which are commonly used in oil production operations. For this purpose, flocculation tests (jar tests) were performed on oil in water emulsions prepared with different oil concentrations. The results showed that the demulsifier alone reduced the oil removal efficiency of the flocculants. Conversely, the presence of SPAM alone further reduced the performance of the flocculants, at both oil concentrations tested. When used together, these additives almost completely suppressed the action of the flocculants. Particle size analyses confirmed that the most efficient flocculant promoted the formation of larger aggregates, while the presence of the demulsifier and SPAM limited this formation. Interfacial tension measurements showed that the flocculants’ action was directly related to the availability of interfacial area, being impaired when this interface was previously occupied by demulsifier and SPAM.

item.title: Enhancing Drug Delivery and Efficacy in Stroke via Supramolecular Nanoparticle Systems
item.description:
Abstract
The pathogenesis of ischemic stroke involves multiple pathological links, such as blood–brain barrier (BBB) disruption, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammation, making comprehensive intervention via a single drug exceedingly difficult. In this study, we constructed a supramolecular coassembly nanoparticles (UA-Gen NPs) composed of Ursolic acid (UA) and Genistein (Gen), which self-assemble into a stable supramolecular structure driven by intermolecular hydrogen bonding and π-π stacking. This nanoplatform not only significantly improved drug hydrophilicity but also achieved a transformation from simple physical mixing to structural integration. In vitro profiles revealed a distinct pH-responsive and sequential release pattern of the system (“fast-Gen/slow-UA”). Pharmacokinetic studies further demonstrated that this coassembly significantly prolonged blood circulation and synchronized the fates of the two drugs in vivo. In a mouse middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) model, UA-Gen NPs exhibited superior efficacy in alleviating BBB leakage, reducing infarct volume, and improving neurobehavioral outcomes compared to their physical mixture. Serological analyses confirmed its regulation of oxidative stress and systemic inflammation, yielding optimal neuroprotection. At the protein expression level, the nanotherapy significantly inhibited Keap1, upregulated Nrf2, and restored Occludin expression. Altogether, by utilizing drug molecules themselves as structural building blocks, this study engineered a supramolecular nanotherapeutic agent featuring microenvironment-responsive release behavior and sequential drug delivery. This work provides a feasible research strategy to overcome the challenges of combination therapy in complex diseases.

item.title: Novichok A-230: Monitoring of Provisional Airborne Exposure Levels
item.description:
Abstract
A method was developed to monitor vaporous Novichok A-230 using depot area air monitoring system (DAAMS) tubes packed with Tenax-TA sorbent, which were solvent-extracted with methanol; the extract was concentrated via nitrogen evaporation, then analyzed by LC-MS/MS. Provisional concentration values, or Z levels, of A-230 were extrapolated from the general population limit (GPL) airborne exposure levels of VX, due to A-230’s similarity to VX as a low–vapor-pressure nerve agent. This monitoring method was conducted in accordance with all quality control (QC) criteria set forth in the U.S. Army CASARM Quality Assurance Plan, with an average percent recovery of 88%, a limit of quantitation (LOQ) of 0.012 ng/mL, a target action limit (TAL) of 0.041 ng/mL, and an uncertainty in found mass (UIFM) of 16%.
